content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small square pasta parcels filled with creamy cheese and served in a flavorful tomato sauce. The dough is made from wheat flour and eggs, while the filling typically includes ricotta, parmesan and seasonings. The dish originates from Italy, where it is traditionally enjoyed as a first course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ravioli first appeared in medieval Italy and were originally handmade.
There are countless filling variations: meat, fish, vegetables, and even sweet versions with fruit.
The tomato sauce is often prepared from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, garlic and basil.
In Italy ravioli are sometimes served as “tagliatelle” strips, but modern cuisine uses many shapes.
Traditional cooking involves boiling in salted water until they float, usually 3–5 minutes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The cheese filling provides a good source of complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Creamy cheese supplies calcium that supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are high in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the dough and cheese deliver B1, B2 and B12 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The dish contains no added sugars, making it suitable for moderate carbohydrate intake.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains salt; those monitoring sodium should choose a low‑salt version.

items.title: Gluten in the pasta
items.content: Traditional wheat flour dough contains gluten, making the dish unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese and oil in the sauce increase the calorie count; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve ravioli hot, drizzled with tomato sauce. Sprinkle with grated parmesan, fresh basil or a drizzle of olive oil. They pair well with a light salad or vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh ravioli should be kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Frozen ravioli can be stored up to 3 months; they can be cooked directly from frozen without thawing.
